statement: A club has $10$ juniors and $12$ seniors. A committee is formed by choosing some of the juniors and the same number of seniors, and it must have at least one member. How many different committees are possible?

choices.misconception: I used the identity that a sum of squares of binomial coefficients is C(2n, n) with n = 10, as if there were also 10 seniors, so I got C(20, 10) - 1.
I found the sum C(22, 12) = 646646 correctly but did not remove the empty committee, which has no members.
I assumed the sum equals the middle coefficient C(22, 11) = 705432 and then removed the empty committee.
I chose the juniors and the seniors independently, 2^10 times 2^12 ways, removed the empty committee, and ignored the condition that the two numbers must match.

hints: Adding up $\binom{10}{k}\binom{12}{k}$ term by term is slow. Look for one choice that describes a whole committee at once.
Describe a committee by the juniors who are on it together with the seniors who are not on it.

With $k$ juniors and $k$ seniors on the committee, that description is a set of $k + (12 - k) = 12$ of the $22$ club members, and every 12-member set comes from exactly one committee. Then remove the empty committee.

solutions.reliable: A committee with $k$ juniors and $k$ seniors can be chosen in $\binom{10}{k}\binom{12}{k}$ ways, so before removing the empty committee the count is $\sum_{k=0}^{10}\binom{10}{k}\binom{12}{k} = \sum_{k=0}^{10}\binom{10}{k}\binom{12}{12-k}$. The right-hand sum counts the ways to choose $12$ of the $22$ club members, split by how many of them, $k$, are juniors (Vandermonde's identity), so it equals $\binom{22}{12} = 646646$. The only committee with $k = 0$ is empty, so the answer is $646646 - 1 = 646645$. Transferable idea: a sum of products of binomial coefficients whose lower indices add to a constant collapses to a single binomial coefficient.
solutions.elegant: Match each committee with the set made of its juniors and the seniors left off it. If the committee has $k$ of each, this set has $k + (12 - k) = 12$ members. Conversely, any 12 of the 22 members, say $k$ juniors and $12 - k$ seniors, give back the committee of those $k$ juniors and the other $k$ seniors. So committees, including the empty one, correspond to 12-member sets: $\binom{22}{12} = 646646$, and removing the empty committee leaves $646645$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
